subtitle: flip the coin...ideals
body: Sooo, what's up with all of this? Once upon a time the Middle Ages ended and the golden age of the Renaissance began, and people got obsessed with ideals, an obsession you can see directly in the way they painted. Raphael's School of Athens is the textbook definition of linear perspective, where every straight line in the architecture, answers to one perspectivity point.

In the fresco, we can draw two horizontal lines across the architecture, at the center each one has a perspectivity point. The lower perspectivity point (orange), sits roughly at head height, with the crowd gathered at the steps. The upper perspectivity point (blue) sits approximately where the vault of the ceiling begins to curve.

You can either follow the blue lines down into the crowd, the floor tiles, the base of the columns, and every one of them, no matter where it starts, narrows back to that lower point or decide to follow the red lines instead, and they narrow back to the upper one, Each of these points is holding a family of lines together.
closing: Remember above, "to determine a line, we need two points, and that two lines will eventually meet somewhere"? That's directly **Axiom 1**, each pair of distinct points is joined by a unique line, and **Axiom 2**, any two lines meet in at least one point, including parallel lines meeting at perspectivity points. The blue and red lines converging at the lower perspectivity point (orange) and upper perspectivity point (blue) are the physical manifestation of these axioms on the canvas.

The crowd with the scattered figures across the fresco provide the non-degenerate space required by **Axiom 3**, ensuring there are at least four distinct points that do not all collapse into a single line.

Looking at the geometric grids of the floor tiles and architectural framing, one could draw complete quadrangles whose diagonal points would maintain proper, non-collinear projective separation, as described in **Axiom 4**.

Any two triangles built from points already sitting on those converging lines are automatically perspective from that point. **Axiom 5** promises that their corresponding sides will always meet at three points lying on a single line, no matter which points along the lines the triangles happen to be built from.

**Axiom 6** is harder to point at directly, since it's a statement about transformations rather than a fixed scene, but it's the reason a perspective construction like this one is rigid at all. Once you know where any three points on one of these lines actually sit, every other point on that same line is already decided. There's no freedom left to place it anywhere else and still have the geometry hold together.
This rigidity creates a fixed illusion for the observer, because the eye focuses on the perspectivity points and sinks the observer into the painting.
